NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Meta.ConfigLabel: Spatial Module Framework - Cages, Pads and Type Defaults
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Meta.ConfigNote: Shared geometry and behaviour for every spatial module, then per-type defaults. A module type registers itself in NaAudio__Spatial__ModuleRegistry and reads its defaults from the TypeDefaults block here, so a new module never hard-codes its own footprint.

NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Shell.ShellNote: The manifest specifies that each module lives inside a bounding box which becomes visible on all six sides when locked. That box is the module SHELL: a pad it stands on, a wireframe cage around it, and a name plate above it. The shell is framework-owned - a module type only ever fills the volume inside it.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Shell.PadShapeNote: rounded | circle | square. A rounded plate under each module is what seats it visually on the floor; without it a module reads as hovering and the space loses its ground.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Shell.HoverLiftNote: The module rises a few centimetres under the cursor. Cheap, immediate, and it removes any doubt about which of several overlapping modules the pointer has.

NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Layout.LayoutNote: Placement rules used when a module is added without an explicit position. Modules are laid out on a ring rather than a grid, because a ring keeps every module the same distance from the listener at the centre and that is the spatial metaphor the whole application rests on.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Layout.MinimumSeparationNote: Cages must not intersect. Two overlapping cages make the lock state unreadable and make picking ambiguous.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Layout.CentreKeptClearNote: The middle of the ring is the listener position and the master bus. Nothing is ever placed there.

NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.PatchGraphNote: The 3D noodles from the manifest. A cable is a swept tube along a cubic Bezier that leaves each socket along the socket's own axis before it droops, with a moulded plug at each end and a sprung slack so it swings when a module is dragged.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.CableGroundHeightNote: The height a lead runs at once it has left its socket. Leads lie on the ground and go AROUND the space rather than arcing over it - a patch bay you look down on rather than a cat's cradle strung between the instruments. This is the single number that decides that.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.CableLeadOutNote: How far a lead runs straight out of a socket before it starts to bend, in metres, capped at a third of the span so a short hop does not overshoot. This one detail is what makes a cable read as plugged into something rather than drawn between two points.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.CableRadialSegmentsNote: Six is a hexagonal barrel. At this radius nothing above eight is distinguishable, and the count multiplies through every length segment of every cable in the space.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.CableSpringNote: A damped spring chasing the rest sag, which is what makes a dragged module swing its leads instead of redrawing them. Raising stiffness without raising damping gives a cable that oscillates for several seconds and reads as broken.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.CableFlowNote: Signal presence is shown by the lead brightening with the source module's meter. A silent cable is visibly still, which is how the user finds a broken patch without opening anything.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.PortRadiusNote: Small. A socket is a detail on an instrument, not a feature of it - at the first size they read as bollards stuck to the side of each module. They only need to be big enough to hit in wiring mode, where nothing else in the scene is competing for the click.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.PortStandoffNote: How far the socket sits proud of the pad rim. Nearly flush - a standoff big enough to see is a socket floating beside the module rather than mounted on it.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.PortHeightNote: Absolute, not a fraction of cage height. Sockets sit just above the pad on every module, so a lead leaves at floor level and runs along the ground. As a fraction of cage height a tall module put its socket up in the air and its leads flew over everything.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.PortRestOpacityNote: How present a socket is outside wiring mode. Visible, so a module still reads as a device with sockets, but plainly not the thing being worked on. Hiding them entirely was the first attempt, and it made switching into wiring mode pop three dozen objects into existence at once.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.GhostCableEmissiveNote: The lead in hand while patching. Tinted to the wiring pigment and lit, rather than made transparent - an opaque cable in the wrong colour reads as 'not connected yet', where a see-through one reads as a rendering fault.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__PatchGr.MaxCablesPerInputNote: The manifest wants many inputs feeding one effect. Eight is the point past which the cable bundle stops being legible in 3D, not an engine limit.

NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__GroundF.GroundFieldNote: How large an island of ground a module puts under itself. The shape and softness of the field live in Na__Env3d__Config; only the per-module sizing is here, because it is a property of being a module.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__GroundF.RadiusNote: radius = max(cage x, cage z) * RadiusFromFootprint * the type's FieldRadiusFactor + RadiusPadding. The padding is what lets two modules a couple of metres apart merge at all - without it an island stops at the edge of its own pad and nothing ever joins up.

NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__LockSta.LockStateNote: Working and locked, per the manifest. Locked silences and disconnects the module's generators; the eventual behaviour also plays back a rendered bounce and loops a captured animation, and the hooks for both are already in NaAudio__Spatial__LockState__.mjs.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__LockSta.TransitionNote: The cage fades in and the body desaturates over this window rather than snapping. A snap reads as a glitch; a fade reads as a state change.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__LockSta.AnimationFreezeOnLockNote: A locked module keeps its last animation pose and stops advancing. When the bounce-and-replay path lands this becomes a looped capture instead, which is what the manifest asks for.

OutputPost.TypeNote: The single exit from the space. Its audio input IS the master bus, so anything patched into it - in series, in parallel, in any arrangement - is what reaches the speakers, and anything with no path to it is silent. That one rule is what makes the signal flow in this space readable by eye.
OutputPost.HasOutputNote: A post has nowhere to send anything. An output socket here would invite a lead out of the speakers and back into the space, which is a feedback loop with a friendly face on it.
OutputPost.IsMasterOutputNote: Read by the patch graph to warn about a space with no route to the speakers - the one broken patch that is completely invisible and completely silent.
OutputPost.FieldRadiusFactorNote: The post stands at the centre and holds the middle of the space open, so its island is deliberately larger than its footprint would give it.
OutputPost.ColumnHeightNote: The master level column standing on the post, scaled on Y by the master meter. Full height is a signal at the limiter.

CircularSequencer.HasInputNote: A sequencer is a source. It has no audio input, so it gets no input socket - a socket you can plug into that carries nothing is worse than no socket, because the lead draws and the connection looks made. When the manifest's trigger cables land this becomes a trigger input rather than an audio one.
CircularSequencer.TypeNote: The manifest's radical departure from the linear step sequencer. Steps sit on a circle, a marker sweeps like a clock hand at the project tempo, and the division count is free rather than locked to sixteen.
CircularSequencer.DivisionsNote: Free division count is the entire point - 3 gives triplets over a beat, 7 gives something no grid sequencer can express without a fight.
CircularSequencer.StepShapesByLaneNote: Different geometric shapes signify different drum sounds, straight from the manifest. Colour alone is not enough - it fails at distance and it fails for anyone with a colour vision deficiency.
CircularSequencer.StepInactiveOpacityNote: Inactive steps are genuinely transparent, not merely smaller. Size alone was not enough: at working distance a ring of sixteen small solid shapes still reads as sixteen active steps, so the pattern was unreadable from anywhere but directly overhead.
CircularSequencer.StepVelocitySizeNote: Multipliers on the active step size, reserved for per-step velocity. The scaling path is wired and every step already carries a Velocity of 1.0; what is missing is the interaction to change it. See the velocity note in the module header.
CircularSequencer.StartMarkerNote: A triangle outside the outer ring pointing inward at division zero. Without it a circular pattern has no readable beginning - which is fine while the marker sweeps, and useless when the transport is stopped.
CircularSequencer.ExpandedWidthFactorNote: Pressing the corner button doubles the base along X and reveals the control bank in the new half. Collapsed, a sequencer is a compact disc on the floor; expanded, it is a workbench. The controls are only built once, and hidden rather than rebuilt, so expanding is free.
CircularSequencer.ControlBankInsetNote: Raised from 0.42 when the sliders turned horizontal - each row now carries its legend at the head of its track, so the bank extends further back toward the module than its origin suggests.
CircularSequencer.ControlBankNote: Five controls in the expanded half: cycle length, grid feel, wobble depth, wobble likelihood and sound bank.
CircularSequencer.CycleDetentsNote: Bars per full revolution of the circle. The whole ring always represents one cycle, so this is the single control that decides how fast the pattern reads - and because it is quantised to bar fractions the sequencer stays locked to the project tempo at every setting.
CircularSequencer.GridDetentsNote: Timing feel. Applied as a per-step offset AND to the step's visual angle together, so where a step SITS on the circle is always where it PLAYS - the module would be lying otherwise. Regular is even; On-Beat pulls every step onto its nearest beat; Triplet pushes every second step to two thirds of its pair; Dotted pushes it to three quarters.
CircularSequencer.WobbleNote: Wow and flutter, as a worn record player has. Depth is how far a step may be dragged early or late, as a fraction of one step; Chance is how often it happens at all. Both are needed - depth alone applies to every step and is just a wonky grid, chance alone does nothing. The offset also detunes the sample slightly, because a real platter changing speed changes pitch, and without that it reads as a timing bug rather than as a machine.
CircularSequencer.WobbleSeedNote: Seeded from the module seed and the absolute step index, so a given step in a given bar always wobbles the same way. A fresh random per playback would make the pattern impossible to learn, which is the opposite of groove.
CircularSequencer.KitDetentsNote: Four positions, a placeholder for a real sound bank browser. A lane binds to a voice ROLE rather than an asset id, so switching the whole kit under a pattern leaves every lane pointing at something sensible - see the voice role note in the sample library README.

CubeMod.HasInputNote: A CubeMod drives its own voice and takes no audio in. Same reasoning as the sequencer - it will gain a modulation input, not an audio one.
CubeMod.TypeNote: An XY pad mapped to each of the six faces of a rotatable cube, so one controller carries twelve dimensions instead of two. Rotating the cube brings a different pair of parameters to hand.
CubeMod.RotationSnapNote: The cube always settles square to the camera. A cube resting at a random angle makes its front face unusable as a pad.

DelayCloud.TailDrainSecondsNote: How long the feedback path takes to ramp to silence when the transport stops. Not a hard cut - the tail then dies over its own couple of repeats, which is a musical stop rather than a guillotine. Zero would click.
DelayCloud.TypeNote: An enclosure the user resizes by hand, with sample spheres bouncing inside it. The box dimensions ARE the parameters - length sets reverb decay, width sets delay time, height sets the damping filter - so the shape of the space you can see is the shape of the space you can hear.
DelayCloud.SphereGravityNote: Well below real gravity. Earth-rate falling in a 1.5 metre box produces a bounce rate far too fast to hear as discrete taps.
DelayCloud.BounceTapMinIntervalNote: Guards against a sphere settling into a corner and machine-gunning taps at frame rate.

NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Modes.ModesNote: Build, Play and Wiring, per NaAudio__AppCore__ModeManager. Build moves modules and freezes everything else; Play works the controls and pins the modules; Wiring patches the signal and freezes both. The split exists because a module's pad, its controls and its sockets all sit centimetres apart in a space the user orbits, so reaching for one and catching another is the common case - and catching a sequencer step means a silently rewritten pattern.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Modes.DefaultModeNote: Play. The space arrives already arranged and already patched, and the first thing anybody wants is to hear it.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Modes.BuildModeGridBoostNote: The ground grid is multiplied by this in Build mode. A layout being rearranged wants a visible measure under it; the same grid during Play is a distraction from the instruments.
NaAudio__SpatialModules__Config__Modes.ControlFadeInBuildNote: Controls dim to this opacity in Build mode. They stay visible so the module still reads as itself, but they are plainly inert - and they are already invisible to the picker, so this is presentation reinforcing behaviour rather than implementing it.
